digests.author: Terry Smith
digests.title: Fundsmith Equity Fund July 2026 half-yearly letter
digests.summary: Terry Smith’s July 2026 half-yearly letter reports Fundsmith Equity Fund returned -2.9% in H1 2026 versus +11.2% for MSCI World (£ net), while since-inception annualised return was +13.1% versus +12.5%. He attributes the backdrop to passive/index funds and the AI boom producing a momentum-dominated market rather than fundamentals. He cites evidence that index funds are concentrated, active funds are a small share of trades, and momentum is at a 30-year high. Smith says Fundsmith will remain focused on good companies at reasonable valuations but will adapt by being more active, accepting potentially higher turnover than its historic average, and taking more account of fundamental and share-price momentum; H1 turnover was 51.8%, which he does not expect to be normal. The letter lists purchases including AppLovin, GE Vernova, Mastercard, Netflix, TSMC and Uber, and exits including LVMH, Novo Nordisk, Unilever and Zoetis. Portfolio characteristics at 30 June 2026 include ROCE 31%, cash conversion 92% and FCF yield 4.3%. Smith warns a reversal could be severe but gives no timing insight.
key_points: Fund returned -2.9% in H1 2026 versus +11.2% for MSCI World (£ net); since inception annualised return was +13.1% versus +12.5%.
Smith says the market is dominated by passive/index funds and the AI boom, producing momentum rather than fundamentals like profitability, returns on capital and growth.
Momentum is described as at a 30-year high and more extreme than in late 1999 before the Dotcom bubble burst.
Fundsmith will be more active, take more account of momentum, and be less willing to buy quality companies on glitches; H1 turnover was 51.8% but should not be the norm.

Purchases included AppLovin, GE Vernova, Legrand, Mastercard, Netflix, Nextpower, Sage, TJX, TSMC, Uber, Veeva and Yum! Brands; exits included Atlas Copco, Coloplast, EssilorLuxottica, Intuit, LVMH, Mettler-Toledo, Nike, Novo Nordisk, Otis, Unilever, Wolters Kluwer and Zoetis.
Portfolio at 30 June 2026: ROCE 31%, gross margin 62%, operating margin 29%, cash conversion 92%, interest cover 43.0x and FCF yield 4.3%.
Smith warns that a momentum reversal could be severe but professes no insight into how or when it will end.

quotes.point: Establishes the fund’s H1 2026 underperformance versus the MSCI World comparator.
quotes.text: Our Fund was down by 2.9% in the first six months of the year

quotes.point: Signals a stated change in Fundsmith’s management approach.
quotes.text: You should therefore expect that we will be more active in future.

quotes.point: Highlights the letter’s warning about momentum extremes.
quotes.text: It is at a 30 year high and more extreme than in late 1999 just before the Dotcom bubble burst.

implications.text: Track the passive/momentum feedback loop and AI concentration described in the letter, including the claim that active funds are now only 10% of trades and momentum is at a 30-year high.
Review North equity exposure to momentum-led and AI-dominated indices; the letter argues index funds are concentrated and not the low-risk diversified portfolios they used to be.
Stress-test reversal and liquidity scenarios, remembering Smith’s warning that the S&P fell 57% in five months in 2007–08 and his speculation that a future reversal could be faster.
The document contains no Indonesia- or IDR-specific analysis; avoid importing its US/UK passive-flow conclusions into the South book without local evidence.

Note Fundsmith’s stated process change: more active management, more attention to momentum and potentially higher turnover, while retaining a quality-and-valuation focus and no desire to hug the index.

digests.author: Prem Watsa
digests.title: Fairfax Financial Holdings Limited 2025 Annual Report — Chairman’s Letter to Shareholders
digests.summary: Fairfax’s 2025 annual report and chairman’s letter report the best year in its history: net income rose to a record $4.8 billion, book value per share increased 21% adjusted for a $15 dividend to $1,260, and the stock rose 31% to Cdn$2,616. Drivers were record underwriting profit of $1.8 billion, record interest and dividend income of $2.6 billion, and net investment gains of $3.2 billion. Since 1985 book value per share has compounded 18.7% annually including dividends, while the stock has compounded 19.5%. Fairfax stresses its decentralized structure and long-term value-oriented investment philosophy. It says the hard market that began in 2019 is now beginning to soften. Consolidated gross premiums were $33.3 billion with a 93% combined ratio, despite $1.2 billion of catastrophe losses mainly from California wildfires; reserves produced redundancies for a 19th year. The investment portfolio was $74.9 billion, fixed income mainly government bonds with 3–4 year maturities, and float was $40.8 billion. The letter also covers ratings upgrades, internal successions, the Eurolife life sale, Kennedy Wilson, and India.
key_points: Record 2025 results: net income $4.8bn; book value per share $1,260, up 21% adjusted for a $15 dividend; stock +31% to Cdn$2,616; underwriting profit $1.8bn; interest/dividend income $2.6bn; net investment gains $3.2bn.

Long-term compounding: since 1985 book value per share compounded 18.7% and stock 19.5% annually including dividends; 2021–2025 book value per share grew 22.5% annually; Fairfax hopes for 15% over time.

Underwriting: gross premiums $33.3bn, consolidated combined ratio 93%, catastrophe losses $1.2bn mainly California wildfires, reserve redundancies for 19 consecutive years totaling $6.9bn; the hard market that began in 2019 is beginning to soften.
Investment portfolio $74.9bn; fixed income mainly government bonds with 3–4 year maturities; cash and short-term treasuries 20% of fixed income; yield 5.0%; $20.5bn common stock holdings.
Float was $40.8bn; gross premiums per share $1,596 and float per share $1,956; shares outstanding fell to 20.9m from 27.8m in 2017 through buybacks.

Ratings: S&P upgraded core insurance financial strength to AA- and debt to A-; AM Best raised Northbridge, Crum & Forster and Allied World to A+; Fitch upgraded debt to BBB+; Moody’s and DBRS positive outlook.

Corporate actions and succession: Eurolife life sale to Eurobank for €813m expected Q2 2026; Kennedy Wilson take-private at $10.90/share accepted; internal successions cited as seamless; AMAG Indonesia is 80.9%-owned.

quotes.point: Signals underwriting-cycle softening despite record 2025 results.
quotes.text: We have benefited greatly from a hard market that began in 2019 but is now beginning to soften.

quotes.point: Defines a government-bond-heavy, short-duration fixed-income posture.
quotes.text: our fixed income portfolio is mainly government bonds (i.e. treasuries) and most carry a term to maturity of 3 – 4 years.

quotes.point: Highlights the scale of insurance float as a long-term funding advantage.
quotes.text: At $40.8 billion, this is a long-term advantage for us.

implications.text: Treat Fairfax’s comment that the 2019 hard market is now beginning to soften as company/industry-cycle evidence; check whether global P&C pricing momentum is fading before extrapolating underwriting margins.

Use the North American insurer disclosures as a peer read: Northbridge combined ratio 89% with gross premiums -5%, Crum & Forster 95% with +9%, Odyssey 94% with +1%, Allied World 89% with +3%, and Zenith 102% with +7% amid workers’ compensation pricing pressure.

Remember AMAG Indonesia is 80.9%-owned by Fairfax: 2025 net premiums written IDR 1,000.2bn (~US$61m), shareholders’ equity IDR 3,142.3bn (~US$188m), 772 employees; the worldwide table also lists AMAG gross premiums $174m, combined ratio 95% and investment portfolio $191m. Do not infer IDR market direction from a parent letter.

Flag that Fairfax’s $20.5bn common stock holdings had $23.6bn market value versus $20.5bn carrying at year-end ($3.1bn gain), and were about $3.7bn above year-end carrying value at February 27, 2026; investment gains remain lumpy even as operating income is steadier.

Use Fairfax’s stated principles—long-term book-value-per-share focus, downside protection and never betting the company—as a checklist for Six South position sizing and holding-period discipline, not as a trading signal.

digests.author: Thomas S. Gayner, Chief Executive Officer
digests.title: Markel 2023 Annual Letter
digests.summary: Tom Gayner’s 2023 Markel annual letter reviews a year he describes as both best and worst of times and argues Markel remains on the path to building “one of the world’s great companies.” The three-engine system—insurance, investments and Markel Ventures—is presented as a resilience and volatility-absorption machine. Ventures and investment operations had excellent results: Ventures EBITDA was $628 million on $4,985 million of revenues, net investment income rose to $735 million from $447 million, and the equity portfolio returned 21.6%. Insurance fell short: the combined ratio was 98% and underwriting profit was $133 million versus $627 million in 2022. Gayner cites management changes, unforced errors in collateralized intellectual property insurance, natural catastrophes and social inflation. He says Markel is tightening terms, lowering limits where appropriate, raising rates, reducing catastrophe exposures and walking away from unprofitable business. Capital allocation includes $445 million of share repurchases and continued equity purchases. Gayner explains “Orange and Blue” intrinsic-value thinking and stresses long-term, low-debt, tax-efficient compounding.
key_points: Markel’s three-engine system—insurance, investments and Markel Ventures—is presented as a resilience and volatility-absorption machine that supports long-term focus.
Insurance fell short of 2023 goals: combined ratio 98% and underwriting profit $133 million versus $627 million in 2022; Gayner cites management changes and tough decisions.
Markel Ventures had a spectacular year: $628 million EBITDA on $4,985 million revenues; since 2005 about $3.7 billion of acquisition checks and about $1.9 billion of cash/dividends.
Investment operations: net investment income rose to $735 million from $447 million; equity portfolio ended at $9.6 billion and returned 21.6%; unrealized equity gain over $6 billion.

Social inflation and catastrophes are key insurance pressures; Markel says it is tightening terms, lowering limits where appropriate, raising rates, reducing catastrophe exposures and walking away from unprofitable business.
Capital allocation: $445 million of buybacks versus $291 million in 2022; $340 million net public equity purchases; Orange and Blue framework guides intrinsic-value and repurchase decisions.

quotes.point: Anchors the letter’s long-term definition of success, useful for judging management against more than one-year results.
quotes.text: We define success as: “building one of the world’s great companies.”

quotes.point: Balances the letter: two engines strong, insurance weak.
quotes.text: In 2023 we earned excellent results in our Markel Ventures and Investment engines. Unfortunately, we fell short of our goals in our Insurance engine.

quotes.point: Signals underwriting discipline in response to social inflation.
quotes.text: We are acting with discipline to walk away from business that doesn’t meet our profitability requirements.

implications.text: Note the letter’s framing of social inflation and catastrophe costs as insurance-market pressures, including rebalancing in states such as California and Florida.
If Markel is in the global book, separate the 2023 insurance shortfall from strong Ventures and investment results; monitor combined ratio and social-inflation actions.
Treat this as Markel-specific; the document contains no direct Indonesia or IDR market read-across.
Track disclosed underwriting profit, combined ratio and catastrophe/social-inflation language as risk checkpoints; Markel says it is reducing exposures and tightening terms.
Use the three-engine and Orange/Blue frameworks as a quality checklist, while remembering Gayner says insurance results will take time to improve.

digests.author: Thomas S. Gayner
digests.title: Markel 2024 Annual Letter
digests.summary: Markel’s 2024 annual letter is a steward’s report from CEO Thomas S. Gayner. He frames Markel as a long-term, diversified “redwood” built on the Markel Style, win-win-win outcomes, local autonomy with accountability, a low-debt balance sheet, frugality and humility. 2024 was “good, but not great”: revenues rose to $16.621 billion from $15.804 billion and operating income to $3.713 billion from $2.929 billion. The insurance combined ratio improved to 95.2% from 98.4%, and insurance operating income rose to $601 million from $348 million, though US specialty faced challenges in construction defects, general liability and risk-managed professional liability. Markel exited several product lines and announced a board-led review focused on specialty insurance. Ventures operating income was flat at $520 million; acquisition prices remain high. Equity investments returned 20.1% versus 25.0% for the S&P 500, and five-year equity returns were 12.8% annually. Fixed income was conservative, with 98% AA-rated or better. Management estimates intrinsic value at $2,610 per share as of December 31, 2024, an 18% five-year CAGR versus 9% for the stock price. The letter also cites 5.4 points of favorable reserve development and a $1.2 billion insurance spread.
key_points: 2024 was 'good, but not great'; operating income rose to $3.713 billion and revenues to $16.621 billion.
Insurance combined ratio improved to 95.2% from 98.4%, but US specialty still had challenges in construction defects, general liability and risk-managed professional liability.
Markel exited several product lines and launched a board-led review focused on its specialty insurance business.
Ventures operating income was flat at $520 million; management remains cautious on acquisition prices.
Equity portfolio returned 20.1% versus 25.0% for the S&P 500; five-year equity return was 12.8% annually.
Management estimates intrinsic value at $2,610 per share, an 18% five-year CAGR versus 9% for the stock price.
Fixed-income portfolio was 98% AA-rated or better; underwriting profit plus net interest income produced a $1.2 billion spread.

quotes.point: Sets a balanced tone and warns against reading the letter as a blanket bullish signal.
quotes.text: it was a good, but not great, year

quotes.point: Supports acquisition caution and capital-deployment discipline in Ventures.
quotes.text: We sense that prices, in general, remain on the high end.

quotes.point: Management’s forward market-return expectation is more cautious than recent results.
quotes.text: Looking towards the next five years, we don’t expect the same sort of overall equity market returns.

implications.text: Remember management expects lower overall equity market returns over the next five years and says acquisition prices remain high; use this as a valuation-discipline input, not a broad forecast.
If Markel is in the North book, track the board-led specialty insurance review and US specialty remediation; management says further 2025 improvement is anticipated after subpar products expire.
No direct Indonesia read-across is stated; do not infer South book actions from Markel’s US specialty issues.
Flag long-tail casualty reserve risk: 2024 had 5.4 points favorable development after 2023/2022 fourth-quarter deficiencies; monitor reserve adequacy and underwriting changes.
Adopt the letter’s long-horizon scorekeeping: judge value creation over five years and against intrinsic-value growth, not one-year equity returns or the expense ratio alone.

digests.author: Thomas S. Gayner
digests.title: 2025 Annual Letter to Our Business Partners
digests.summary: Markel’s 2025 annual letter, written by CEO Thomas S. Gayner, frames the company as a “home” anchored by culture and long-term compounding. Quantitatively, Gayner reports 12% growth in intrinsic value per share in 2025, 15% compound annual growth over five years and 16% since IPO. Operating revenues rose to $15.5bn from $14.8bn, while operating income fell to $3.2bn from $3.7bn; the combined ratio improved to 94% from 95%. Markel Insurance promoted Simon Wilson to CEO and reorganized around accountable P&Ls; it reported $484m of reserve redundancies, or 5.8 points, and sold reinsurance renewal rights to refocus on specialty underwriting. Fixed income returned 3.5%, and Gayner says Markel avoids “private credit” and riskier credit. Industrials revenues were $3.9bn with adjusted operating income of $343m versus $365m amid K-shaped end-markets. Public equities returned 10.5%; Markel repurchased 223,000 shares at an average $1,894 and redeemed $600m of preferred. Gayner flags tougher economic conditions and softer property insurance prices as near-term pressures but remains confident in long-term profitability and conservative reserving.
key_points: Intrinsic value per share grew 12% in 2025, 15% CAGR over five years and 16% since IPO, by Markel’s consistently applied method.
Operating revenues rose to $15,513 million from $14,814 million, but operating income fell to $3,195 million from $3,713 million; combined ratio improved to 94% from 95%.
Markel Insurance promoted Simon Wilson to CEO and reorganized to give each operation an accountable P&L; 2025 reserve redundancies were $484 million, or 5.8 points.

Markel sold reinsurance renewal rights to refocus on specialty underwriting, expecting lower total revenues and temporary expense-ratio headwinds but improved Markel Insurance combined ratio and return on equity.
Fixed income returned 3.5%; Gayner says Markel buys high-quality fixed income and avoids “private credit” and riskier credit securities.
Industrials revenues were $3.9 billion and adjusted operating income $343 million versus $365 million, with management citing K-shaped end-markets and an unwinding transportation-equipment cycle.

Public equities returned 10.5%; Markel bought 223,000 shares at average $1,894, redeemed $600 million preferred, and had $8.9 billion unrealized equity gains and nearly $2 billion deferred tax liability at a 22% tax rate.

quotes.point: Signals a risk-first equity discipline rather than short-term performance chasing.
quotes.text: We invest to avoid permanent capital loss

quotes.point: Highlights Markel’s conservative fixed-income credit stance and explicit avoidance of riskier credit.
quotes.text: we do not take risks like the currently popular “private credit” options or riskier credit securities.

quotes.point: Near-term headwind acknowledgment despite continued long-term confidence.
quotes.text: tougher economic conditions and softer property insurance prices may pressure reported results.

implications.text: Remember management’s near-term flags: tougher economic conditions, softer property insurance prices, and K-shaped industrial end-markets; treat these as US/global cycle signals only.

Use Markel’s insurance reorganization, reserve redundancies, and reinsurance exit as a read-across for North specialty-insurance and underwriting-quality checks; do not extrapolate directly to the IDR book.
Review our own credit and reserve assumptions against Gayner’s “balance sheet first” stance and his explicit avoidance of private credit and riskier credit securities.
No Indonesia/IDR content appears in this letter; do not infer South book actions from Markel’s US insurance and industrial commentary without local data.

Track Markel’s capital allocation—buybacks at an average $1,894, $600 million preferred redemption, and $8.9 billion unrealized equity gains—as a long-duration compounding case study, not a trading signal.
